items.title: Palestinians and US journalist injured by Israeli settlers in West Bank harvest attack
items.summary: The BBC sees masked settlers attack Palestinians trying to harvest olives, amid a surge in similar incidents.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians in West Bank during olive harvest
By Lucy Williamson Middle East correspondent ,Â  Reporting from Abu Falah
Dozens of masked settlers have attacked Palestinians and set fire to cars and olive trees during the annual olive harvest in the occupied West Bank.
A BBC team witnessed one of several attacks in farmland near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah. A local official said the attacks had injured 12 Palestinians, including four dual Palestinian American citizens. A foreign journalist was also among those hurt.
Driving into the area early in the morning, we came across the first signs of the violence : a stream of cars carrying wounded Palestinian olive farmers racing out along the narrow stony track, piled high with olive picking equipment, as smoke rose from several fires nearby.
The bloodied face of Majdi Fheed peered out from the backseat of one car.
"We were getting our olive trees and almost 15 Jewish guys â¦ started attacking us with guns, with rocks, with special weapons. They hit me on my head [and] my neck â look, I am bleeding!"
Yaser AlKam, a council member from the neighbouring village of Turmus Aya told me Majdi - an American citizen - was attacked by settlers with nail-studded sticks, and needed treatment for deep wounds on his head. His elderly mother was also injured.
Another man ferrying the injured to hospital told us that settlers had attacked them with sticks while they harvested their olives, and had burned three cars â including one of his own.
"As soon as we got to the land and put our things on the ground, they started to come, so we ran away" said a woman next to him.
Image caption, Several Palestinian-American citizens and a foreign journalist were left injured following the attack
Asked about the violence, a US State Department spokesperson said they were aware of the reports.
"Weâ¯condemn criminalâ¯violenceâ¯by any partyâ¯in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests, and convictions,â¯of those responsible," the spokesperson said.
Watching the vehicles stream past her, 73-year-old Imm Khaldoun told me emphatically that, no matter what happened, she would always return to her land. "This is my land. It's my right [to be here]" she told me.
The UN says the past two weeks have already seen more attacks by violent Israeli settlers than during the entire harvest season last year.
Olive picking in the West Bank is now a test of speed, with trees rapidly stripped of fruit as soon as the sun rises, before violent Israeli settlers attack.
In another olive orchard nearby, we watched as dozens of farmers used power-tools to strip the trees as fast as they could â one eye on the ridge above us, where a group of settlers at a new illegal outpost had already gathered, and were watching the olive harvest below.
Standing on ladders, the Palestinian farmers worked quickly, sending streams of olives onto the plastic sheets laid out under the trees. Three villages had come together to harvest these olives, the landowner Amin Khalil, told me, as a form of protection against attack. He said his land was now surrounded by seven Jewish settlements and outposts.
Image caption, Yaser AlKam was left bloodied from the attack
All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law. Outposts â small encampments on hilltops â are illegal under Israeli law as well, but many still receive state support.
"This is a hotspot â there are seven settlements around here," Amin Khalil told me. "This year, all the people came together because when there are just a few people working alone at the edge of the village, the settlers attack. So all the families are working together today."
But the tactic doesn't work today. As we watch, dozens of settlers, all dressed in black, begin moving down the hill towards us, setting fire to several groups of olive trees.
There are shouts of panic from the Palestinian farmers, yelling for children to get out of the field. Some begin swiftly wrapping up the olives to leave.
But with large numbers of people on both sides, the confrontation stalls into an uneasy stalemate. We see settlers with slingshots hurl stones towards us, and young Palestinian men running to throw stones in return.
As Israeli forces arrive, the standoff explodes into action. Settlers begin running down towards us as the farmers swiftly retreat. Some Palestinians set off fireworks to try and push the settlers back.
Image caption, The UN says settler attacks this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others
American journalist Heidi Levine of the Washington Post was injured in the attack. She described how dozens of settlers ambushed her as she was reporting at the scene.
"I got jumped," she said. "I was on the ground and they were kicking me and I was trying to hold onto my camera and my bag. I had my helmet and flak jacket on which protected me. They made me stand up and they kicked me again, and this went on for at least 10 minutes."
In a statement, Washington Post executive editor Matt Murray said Levine had been clearly identifiable as a journalist.
"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," he said.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said personnel had been despatched to the area "following a report of a violent confrontation". It said a female journalist had been injured during the confrontation. And that "all circumstances" surrounding the incident would be examined.
As the farmers retreated, the sound of live ammunition cracked across the fields. It was unclear if settlers or Israeli forces were firing.
Minutes later, Israeli forces began firing tear gas into the Palestinian fields to end the confrontation â a well-worn Israeli pattern of managing these conflicts.
The UN says settler attacks on the olive harvest this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others across the West Bank.
Illegal Jewish outposts have mushroomed here over the past few years, clustering in closer around Palestinian olive groves.
What we witnessed was part of a pattern being repeated day after day, as settler outposts here increase.
The yearly olive harvest has become a litmus test of how the policies of Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government are affecting Palestinians here, by presiding over growing violence by extremist settlers, and fuelling Jewish claims to the land.

items.title: The Victory of Asymmetry in the Iran War - Council on Foreign Relations
items.summary: The Victory of Asymmetry in the Iran War  Council on Foreign Relations
items.content:
In the day-to-day of the Iran war, it’s natural to feel a touch of whiplash. Are we on the verge of agreement or at the dawn of escalation? Is Iran on the edge of collapse, or is it expanding the conflict? Will the Strait of Hormuz return to the status quo ante, or will tolling and periodic attacks on shipping be the new normal? These are important issues but there are larger, more fundamental strategic shifts underway as well. Not since 9/11 and the U.S. invasion of Iraq has the Middle East been in this degree of strategic flux.
It’s been nearly eight months since the war started, two hundred and thirty days to be precise, and, checking the tactical as well as the strategic report card, the record is decidedly mixed.
At the start of the conflict, the Trump administration sought to lay out its objectives. As Undersecretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby put it at an event at the Council within a week of the war’s start: “The president has directed the United States Armed Forces to conduct a military campaign with a focus on degrading and destroying the Islamic Republic of Iran’s ability to project military power in the region, and potentially beyond.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio specified the objectives in even greater detail: “Number one, the destruction of their air force. Number two, the destruction of their navy. Number three, the severe diminishing of their missile launching capability. And number four, the destruction of their factories so they can’t make more missiles and more drones to threaten us in the future.”
On the basis of these goals, the war has achieved much of what it set out to do. By any measure, Iran has fewer military capabilities and a more strained economy than it had before. Iran’s navy sits at the bottom of the ocean, as the Trump administration likes to say, and its missile capabilities have been significantly degraded.
These results, of course, have not come without cost. Tragically, the lives of twenty-one U.S. service members have been lost, as well as over a thousand Iranian civilians. Additionally, the United States has spent down important munitions needed for its other key strategic commitments and priorities. By depleting Patriot interceptors and THAAD batteries, the United States faces increased challenges to maintain its force posture elsewhere around the world including, crucially, in the Indo-Pacific.
More broadly, though, if the goal of Operation Epic Fury was to prevent Iran from projecting power beyond its borders, it might well have had the opposite effect.
The most significant outcome of the war may well prove to be the power of asymmetry. Tehran knew when the war began that it lacked the direct firepower to defeat the United States, but it discovered that, with relatively few missiles, drones, and mines, it could turn its greatest asset—control over the Strait of Hormuz—into a powerful economic weapon that allows it to project power, at least for now, across the global economy.
The resulting repercussions on energy prices, inflation, and affordability in the United States led U.S. President Donald Trump to strike an agreement last week with Russian President Vladimir Putin to allow the sale of millions of barrels of Russian diesel. That sale, protested by Europeans and Ukrainians alike, is pouring more money into the coffers of the Russian war machine and has opened a U.S. rift with Europe and Ukraine, further complicating any path to ending that destructive and intractable war.
The long arm of Iran is also being felt in the country fields of England. Amid fears of a possible state-sponsored terrorist attack on the RAF Fairford base, the United States removed its long-range B–1 bombers, which played a key role in the war in Iran. Iran had previously attempted to reach out beyond its borders to assassinate dissidents as well as foreign officials involved in the 2020 attack on Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps General Qasem Soleimani, but a potential attack on a military base of a NATO ally may be one of the most striking examples of Iran’s sense of confidence despite the hits it has taken since February.
Back in Iran’s backyard, this week has also seen a significant escalation in the war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen. Just on Saturday, Houthi attacks on the international airport in Riyadh killed more than a dozen people and injured over three hundred more. This exchange of rockets is coming at a particularly precarious time for Saudi Arabia as a model of safety and stability in the region. On Monday, senior global energy executives from Chevron, ExxonMobil, Shell, BP, and TotalEnergies canceled their travel to Riyadh where they were scheduled to attend the WPC Energy Congress, a major energy conference.
The kingdom is set to host another big global event in ten days: its annual Future Investment Initiative conference, dubbed “Davos in the Desert.” This gathering of major capital allocators and heads of state is a crucial component of Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s high-profile, long-term modernization plan to shift the economy away from over-dependence on energy exports and toward technology, tourism, and entertainment. On the current trajectory, it would not surprise me if flights into Riyadh, assuming the airport is open, are half-empty at best.
To think that the poorly funded but scrappy Houthis are able to upset a multi-trillion-dollar, multi-decade strategy of one of the richest countries in the world is another example of the might of asymmetry. But it is the potential impact of this conflict on the United States’s regional strategy that could loom much larger.
For a long time, Iran has wanted to push the United States out of the region. Over the years, though, the United States increased its presence across thirteen bases in partner countries, including Bahrain, Kuwait, and Qatar, in order to deter aggression, promote stability, and preposition assets for conflicts as they arise.
As CFR’s Steven Cook has noted, Iran has turned the logic of those bases on its head. Partner countries initially sought U.S. bases as a source of security; now they are targets because of them. They assumed that the United States would actively defend them should Iran or its proxies attack; now that is open to question. After Iranian strikes damaged these bases, the United States withdrew certain forces, even as it deployed more mobile capabilities as part of a third carrier strike group and an additional Marine Expeditionary Unit. If and when the dust of this conflict settles, will partner countries want to rebuild those bases and have U.S. forces return to them? The long and drawn-out process of winding down the costly wars the United States has fought in the region for more than three decades will almost certainly be accelerated by this one.
And who or what would take the United States’ place? A drawdown of U.S. forces in the region would likely set off a frantic realignment of Middle Eastern politics and alliance networks. Without the U.S. security umbrella that so many of our regional partners thought they could depend on, they may turn to others, and each other, for that security. In the best case, that looks like a Middle Eastern NATO: an alliance or perhaps a lattice of alliances of like-minded neighbors committed to their collective security.
The recent Mecca Joint Defense Agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey transforming into a more operational grouping is one possibility; another is the Abraham Accords, which tied Bahrain, Israel, Morocco, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) closer together. And how will those countries seek to guarantee their security? Potentially through the pursuit of nuclear weapons. Given that the purpose of the initial strikes against Iran was to prevent nuclear proliferation in this region, it’s ironic that we may end up seeing additional countries in the region, including Saudi Arabia and the UAE, ultimately pursuing nuclear weapons capabilities.
And what is to come for Iran in this brave new world? Tehran today is weaker than it’s ever been and stronger than it almost certainly expected to be—both at the same time. How do you negotiate with a regime that is keenly aware of that? There is reporting that the United States might be planning for an escalation of attacks and that the Iranian regime is increasingly fragile. That said, the regime has proven more resilient than many expected, as has the Iranian economy, or at least the capacity of the Iranian people to absorb economic pain. This regime could well be a long-term participant in the future of Middle Eastern geopolitics, one that we might all have to learn to live with.

IEA Moves to Accelerate Oil Reserve Releases as Hormuz Crisis Drags On
The International Energy Agency (IEA) has agreed to accelerate the release of approximately 100 million barrels of emergency oil stocks, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel, as the prolonged Strait of Hormuz crisis continues to strain global energy supplies.
The decision, announced Thursday following a meeting of the agency's Governing Board, comes amid mounting concerns over diesel shortages, high fuel prices and renewed attacks on commercial shipping in the Middle East.
According to the IEA's statement , member countries have already released approximately 330 million barrels under the emergency stock release agreed in March in response to the Iran war. The agency said it would take steps to accelerate the remaining releases, with more than 20 million barrels of diesel to be made available as soon as possible.
The original agreement called for a record 400 million barrels of oil and petroleum products. However, some member countries have released more than initially pledged, while others plan to do the same, meaning the final total is expected to exceed 400 million barrels.
The latest decision primarily speeds up previously committed releases rather than establishing an entirely new emergency stock drawdown. The IEA did not provide a specific timetable for completing the releases.
The renewed push comes as the agency warns that the global diesel shortage could persist well into 2027.
In its October Oil Market Report , published Wednesday, the IEA said disruptions to production and exports from the Middle East and Russia removed approximately 1.3 million barrels per day of diesel and gasoil exports from the market in September compared with a year earlier.
While crude oil shipments from the Persian Gulf have recovered significantly from their lows earlier in the conflict, refined petroleum product exports remain severely constrained.
Middle Eastern refined product shipments averaged 1.9 million barrels per day in September, compared with 4.7 million barrels per day before the war. Meanwhile, total oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz reached 10.9 million barrels per day during September, supported by increased tanker movements and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman.
Attacks on commercial vessels have intensified in October, including the sinking of the Singapore-flagged containership GFS Pride after it was struck by a projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz.
The continued disruption is also eroding global oil inventories. The IEA estimates that observed oil stocks at the end of September were 509 million barrels below their pre-war levels, leaving the market with reduced protection against further supply shocks.
Despite a rebound in Gulf crude exports, the agency expects constrained diesel supplies and elevated transportation costs to continue weighing on global energy markets. It forecasts global oil demand will decline by 2.6 million barrels per day in 2026 as higher prices and weaker economic activity take their toll.
The Governing Board also called on member countries with oil production and refining capacity to increase supplies, particularly diesel, and emphasized the importance of maintaining the free flow of energy trade.
The IEA said it would continue monitoring the emergency releases and provide further recommendations to G7 leaders based on updated market assessments, with particular attention to diesel supplies.

‘Tough to watch, impossible to ignore’: reviewers on NAZA documentary
Film interviewing military insiders about mass killing of civilians in Gaza wins widespread praise around the world
Critics around the world have hailed the award-winning documentary NAZA as a “brilliant and harrowing” film that is “impossible to ignore”.
NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, was released in UK cinemas this week and will be shown in more than 50 countries. As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November.
The investigative documentary, which contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders speaking anonymously on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night, has received widespread praise.
In a five-star review, the Financial Times’s Danny Leigh says that as a piece of cinema, “journalism and film-making brilliantly entwine”. The Times calls the film “hugely provocative and a disturbing account” of Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, and the Irish Times brands NAZA an “essential record of engineered nightmare”. In a four-star review, the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw says the “ anguish of Gaza is brought into pin-sharp focus ”.
British Vogue calls NAZA a “brilliant and harrowing film” that outlines the “restrained, meticulous, bone-chilling depiction of the progressive erasure of Gaza”. The magazine says the film “feels destined to become an enduring historical document, one which will and should be seen by generations to come”.
Time Out magazine says NAZA “puts together a restrained, intelligent, articulate, precise and utterly damning case against Israel’s actions in Gaza and their ongoing actions through the region. As a work of cinema, it is exemplary. As a work of journalism, it is inarguable. As a document, it is an indictment.”
The New York Times makes the film a “critic’s choice” and calls NAZA a “haunting” documentary that is “tough to watch, and impossible to ignore”. The Los Angeles Times says NAZA is a “stone-cold frightening” film that “burns the conscience”. And in New York magazine, it is described as “one of the most important films of our time”.
NAZA: the film Israel does not want you to see - video
The Hollywood Reporter praises NAZA as a “sober and thoroughly documented bombshell of an exposé” that “leaves one with a deadening feeling, as if humanity may have lost all hope”. The Toronto Star says “NAZA is heartbreaking but essential viewing, questioning the systems that cause and quantify civilian death in modern warfare”.
The Spanish outlet El Mundo hailed NAZA as “the film of our time, a superb, electrifying, and devastating documentary about the systematic model of annihilation of the Palestinian people” that ultimately “points the finger at us. At night, in silence.”
The French newspaper Le Monde says the film “has the effect of an uppercut that leaves the viewer stunned”, while the Danish culture magazine Soundvenue calls NAZA a “soul-crushing testimony to the genocide in Gaza” that is an “example of how the world increasingly seems like a dystopia”.
The United Arab Emirates’ state-owned newspaper the National calls NAZA a “sickeningly tough film to watch”, and an editorial in the Israeli-outlet Haaretz says the film is “trying to force Israelis to confront what they already know: that Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza has left a black stain”.
When the film opened in Italy last month, it topped the charts . The Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera says NAZA lasts “only 80 minutes, but no more is needed: the ‘scientific’ coldness with which the interviewees reconstruct how they are destroying Gaza is something unforgettable”.
The film contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders who detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge that large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.
Various organisations, including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based, have said Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
The film premiered at the Venice film festival, where it was received a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went on to win the special jury prize .

Taiwan Semiconductor Holds the Cards As NVIDIA, Apple and AMD Battle for Limited AI Chip Capacity
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Ltd. (NYSE: TSM ) remains at the center of the global artificial intelligence boom as major technology companies compete for limited chipmaking and advanced-packaging capacity.
The chipmaker is expanding production to meet long-term demand. However, supply constraints remain a growing concern for customers racing to build AI infrastructure.
Taiwan Semiconductor shares have gained nearly 40% in 2026, compared with a more than 60% increase in the PHLX Semiconductor Index .
Taiwan Semiconductor reported third-quarter revenue of $46.7 billion, up 16.2% sequentially and above the high end of its guidance .
Gross margin fell 1.3 percentage points sequentially to 66.4%, partly reflecting the initial production ramp of its 2-nanometer technology.
Meanwhile, high-performance computing revenue jumped 22% sequentially, accounting for 68% of total sales.
Chips manufactured using 7-nanometer and more advanced processes represented 79% of wafer revenue, highlighting strong demand for leading-edge technology.
Competition for Taiwan Semiconductor’s manufacturing capacity is intensifying as major technology companies seek to secure AI chip supplies.
Mizuho Securities Managing Director Jordan Klein told CNBC on Thursday that competition is particularly fierce among major customers, including Broadcom, NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ: NVDA ), Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL ) and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ: AMD ).
Taiwan Semiconductor North America President Sajiv Dalal said he receives at least 10 calls daily from customers seeking wafer capacity.
Klein said the company could increase capacity by 10% to 20% beyond earlier targets, potentially reaching 120,000 wafers per month by year-end.
He expects NVIDIA and Apple to secure a significant share of the additional supply.
Limited manufacturing capacity could complicate the technology industry’s aggressive AI investment plans.
Klein warned that shortages of advanced logic chips could threaten ambitious revenue projections for frontier AI models and large-scale infrastructure projects.
Vlad Galabov , co-host of The AIDC Debate, said advanced logic chip shortages differ from memory constraints because these processors require customized designs and long-term production planning.
As a result, even major customers such as NVIDIA, Advanced Micro Devices and Apple face supply risks.
Taiwan Semiconductor’s 10 largest customers accounted for 78% of its 2025 net revenue, according to CNBC.
Beyond wafer production, advanced packaging has emerged as another major constraint.
Galabov said NVIDIA has already reserved most of Taiwan Semiconductor’s advanced chip-on-wafer-on-substrate, or CoWoS, packaging capacity.
The company is working to double that capacity to meet growing demand for AI processors.
Meanwhile, Klein said Taiwan Semiconductor could accelerate production by installing additional manufacturing equipment rather than waiting for entirely new factories.
The company is also expanding operations in Taiwan, Japan and Arizona. It has committed to ASML Holding N.V. (NASDAQ: ASML )‘s $400 million High-NA EUV technology and is reportedly considering another manufacturing site in Texas.
The capacity crunch is also making it harder for emerging chip designers to secure manufacturing agreements.
Klein said Taiwan Semiconductor evaluates customers based on long-term demand forecasts, target markets and expected production requirements rather than immediate orders alone.
Sid Sheth of dMatrix said the chipmaker remains highly selective and expects customers to provide credible demand projections.
He emphasized that developing competitive products, building relationships and executing consistently are essential to securing production capacity.
Taiwan Semiconductor’s manufacturing constraints could create opportunities for rival chipmakers.
Intel Corp. (NASDAQ: INTC ) and Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. (OTC: SSNLF ) could benefit as customers explore alternative manufacturing partners.
Klein said Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan is working to strengthen manufacturing operations and attract external foundry customers.
Potential customers could include Apple, NVIDIA and companies linked to Elon Musk , although such agreements remain speculative.
For now, strong AI demand continues to reinforce Taiwan Semiconductor’s position in advanced chip manufacturing. However, limited wafer and packaging capacity remains a critical challenge for the broader AI industry.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh warned of a potential "shock" to the U.S. economy delivered by a rise in artificial intelligence spending , pledging to contain price increases as a flood of private sector funds drives up demand.
"If you’re a central banker, you’re in the business of trying to ensure stable prices and full employment, you’ve got to recognize this as a shock," Warsh said in Bangkok, Thailand, at a conference organized by the International Monetary Fund.
A surge in AI spending has helped boost the U.S. economy in recent quarters. In theory, an onrush of investment in activities like chip manufacturing and data center construction could put upward pressure in general on consumer prices, unless the demand is offset by a new supply of goods and services.

Price hikes prompted the Fed to raise interest rates a quarter of a percentage point in September, marking the central bank's first rate increase since 2023.
An increase to the benchmark interest rate aims to slash inflation by slowing the economy and eating away at demand, though the policy typically yields results after a lag time lasting several months.

Many investors appeared to interpret Warsh's posture as a sign the Fed may hold interest rates steady later this month.

Fed's Warsh withholds rate signal, praises recent global tightening
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, in his speech Friday in Bangkok, declined to offer clues on whether there will be an interest rate hike again this month.
He acknowledged a "synchronous tightening" by central banks around the world, saying there are "no free riders."
He expressed optimism that artificial intelligence will make economies that use it well more productive and wealthier, warning the road there will be “very bumpy.”
Fed’s Warsh in Bangkok: 'Not in that business anymore' of broadcasting decisions
BANGKOK — Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh refrained from signaling whether there will be another interest rate hike again this month, while acknowledging a "synchronous tightening" by central banks around the world.
"I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year," Warsh said, reiterating his opposition to the use of forward guidance for markets that should rely on interpreting data.
He also acknowledged that stance may disappoint anyone who had hoped for a steer ahead of the central bank meeting later this month. "It's a new chapter at the Fed [and] we're not in that business anymore," he said.
Warsh spoke at a fireside chat with the International Monetary Fund's managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, as part of the weeklong IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday.
"Alongside other recent comments from FOMC participants, Warsh's comments indicate that the FOMC is set to pause in October," Goldman Sachs economists led by Jan Hatzius wrote in a note. "We continue to expect a second and final hike in December."
S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures edged higher following the speech, while stock market indexes in Asia and Treasury yields were largely stable.
Chair of the Federal Reserve of the United States Kevin Warsh speaks during the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group annual meetings at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center (QSNCC) in Bangkok, Thailand, on October 16, 2026.
Warsh described the global shift toward tighter monetary policy as a common fight on prices. Central banks made their own choices under their own mandates, he said, but the result was "a synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world," which means "there's no free riders."
Surging energy costs stemming from the Iran war and artificial intelligence investment boom are stoking inflation and pushing up borrowing costs around the world, just as global public debt is on pace to exceed 100% of the world's GDP, a level last breached in the aftermath of World War II.
The U.S. government has insisted that strong growth would be the best way to grow out of its rising debt pile, dismissing IMF's warning that the plans of relying solely on growth won't work as something that needs to be taken "with a grain of salt."
Warsh also expressed optimism about how AI will make economies that use it well more productive and wealthier, while warning the road there may be "very bumpy," and its near-term effect on employment is still uncertain.
"I want you to hear from me optimism, but optimism leavened by the seriousness of purpose," Warsh said.
A decade from now, he said, people will look back on the developments and "say this was hugely consequential."
The Fed raised rates to a range of 3.75% to 4% last month, its first hike since 2023 . Traders see a 72.3% chance for the Fed to keep the interest rate unchanged at the Oct. 27-28 meeting, according to CME FedWatch, while the majority expect a 25 basis point hike at the December meeting.

items.title: China tells Israel to stop 'forced establishment' of West Bank settlements
items.summary: Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi spoke to Israeli President Isaac Herzog on the sidelines of a conference.
items.content:
Image caption, China has been positioning itself as a mediator for conflicts in the Middle East
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has told Israel to stop its "forced establishment" of settlements in the West Bank and reverse its actions, his office said.
The "Palestinian question" is "the greatest historical injustice of this century", Wang told Israeli President Isaac Herzog in a face-to-face meeting on the sidelines of a conference in Azerbaijan on Thursday.
Beijing has been a long-standing supporter of the Palestinian cause and has maintained that a "two-state solution" is the "correct direction".
It has also been positioning itself as a mediator for conflicts in the Middle East.
In 2023 Beijing brokered a deal to restore diplomatic ties between Iran and Saudi Arabia after years of hostility. Earlier this year, it was part of efforts, along with Pakistan, to propose a ceasefire in the US-Israel war against Iran .
Beijing's efforts to tackle the war in Gaza have focused on Palestinian unity.
In 2024 Beijing got rival Palestinian factions to agree to form an interim "national reconciliation government" for the occupied West Bank and Gaza after the war with Israel, although it was never implemented.
Now, Wang says the "immediate priority" is to fully open access to Gaza and stop the continued spread of a "humanitarian catastrophe".
China is willing to work with the international community to get the parties to return to dialogue and "seek a political solution to the conflict", he said.
In a post on X, Herzog said he was "pleased" to meet Wang and their talk "focused on the relations between our countries and the situation in the Middle East".
"I emphasised Israel's desire for peace in the region, alongside the strategic threats to our security, first and foremost from Iran and its terror proxies," he wrote.
China maintains close ties with Iran and is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which had previously come under US sanctions because of Tehran's nuclear programme.
China itself has been accused of trying to dilute its minority populations by encouraging Han Chinese migration to Tibet, which it annexed in the 1950s, and Xinjiang. Beijing rejects those claims, saying its policies promote economic development and social stability.
One year into the ceasefire, people in Gaza continue to live under the regular threat of Israeli strikes, displacement and food security challenges.
Although large-scale bombardment has stopped, Israel has continued strikes in Gaza almost every day . More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli strikes there in the year since the ceasefire started in October 2025, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The US-brokered ceasefire was the first phase of a deal to end the war in Gaza, which had been triggered by a deadly Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.
But progress into the deal's next phase has been stalled, with both Israel and Hamas accusing each other of violating the terms of their agreement.

items.summary: Ukrainian president says US limiting access was a ‘dangerous and unpleasant surprise’, amid reports the order came from inside White HouseEurope live – latest updatesVolodymyr Zelenskyy has said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service has not yet been ful
items.content:
A Ukrainian soldier sets up Starlink satellite internet system near the frontline in Donetsk Photograph: Reuters
A Ukrainian soldier sets up Starlink satellite internet system near the frontline in Donetsk Photograph: Reuters
Starlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says Zelenskyy
Ukrainian president says US limiting access was a ‘dangerous and unpleasant surprise’, amid reports the order came from inside White House
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service has not yet been fully restored, as media reports suggested the order to throttle the service had come from within the White House.
Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels, where he asked the EU for another €70bn (£60bn) next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia.
The meeting offered an important opportunity for Zelenskyy and Europe to align their strategies, as Zelenskyy once again found himself embroiled in a major quarrel with the US president, Donald Trump .
Trump calls Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries ‘a disgrace’
Hours earlier, Trump had called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised ⁠Zelenskyy, after a purported “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold.
“All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher,” Trump told the Newsmax television channel. “Well, I think that’s a disgrace.”
Energy analysts told the BBC that the US-Israeli war on Iran was having the biggest impact on diesel export volumes , although the Ukraine war was also significant.
Trump’s administration is suspected of withholding intelligence from Ukraine on incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes, and of throttling Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite internet network, to prevent it from being used on drones flying faster than 100mph. Neither has officially been confirmed.
Firefighters working at the scene of a Russian drone strike in a residential area in Kyiv on Thursday. Photograph: Vincenzo Circosta/Anadolu/Getty Images Speaking after meeting EU leaders on Friday, Zelenskyy said that Starshield had not yet returned to normal.
“Our defence ministry is in touch and my partners, they told me that there were signals from the White House that they would return these capabilities,” Zelenskyy said. “Have they returned to the previous speed limits? No. But is it coming back now? Yes.”
Reuters on Friday reported that the order to throttle Starshield had come from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a western official briefed on the matter. They did not identify the White House official who had made the decision, but said the Pentagon had been informed that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military had to be slowed.
Zelenskyy called it a “very dangerous and unpleasant surprise” that speeds had been reduced on Starlink, which Ukraine uses to support its most effective air defence systems against Russian jet-powered drones.
Starlink is produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, but controlled by the US government .
When Zelenskyy arrived for talks with EU leaders, he was applauded by the heads of state and government of the bloc’s 27 countries. Zelenskyy later said he had heard “only support”, when asked about reports that European leaders had asked him to dial down his criticism of Trump.
Zelenskyy with the presidents of the European Council, Antonio Costa (left), and the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen (right), on Friday. Photograph: Pier Marco Tacca/Getty Images According to a transcript of his remarks, he told EU leaders that the war would cost €155bn in 2027. “And we need at least €70bn more from you – for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience,” he said. “This is a realistic amount.”
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, agreed with Zelenskyy that “it is clear that we have a gap of €70bn that has to be covered” for 2027, although she expected Ukraine’s other partners – which she did not name – to cover part of the sum.
The EU is currently giving Ukraine regular payments from a €90bn funding plan agreed last December that was intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s civilian and military needs for 2026-27. The remaining third was to be filled by other “international partners”, such as the UK, Canada, Norway and Japan.
The realisation that Kyiv again risks a financial crunch has put Russia’s €210bn assets frozen inside the EU back on the table. The EU takes the profits from those assets to support Ukraine, but last year decided against using the funds themselves, instead opting for an EU-backed €90bn loan.
Belgium, which hosts the vast majority of the Russian funds, remains strongly opposed to using the frozen assets, fearing it will be left to carry the financial burden if the plan goes wrong. But Zelenskyy said there could be an alternative.
“We need something like a special EU-controlled custodian to reduce the risk of them being unfrozen and divided up among those who clearly do not want what is best for Europe or an end to this war,” he said.
The European Commission, a strong backer of last year’s rejected frozen assets plan, has been reluctant to propose new variants – such as an EU-controlled custodian – because it fears running into same opposition from Belgium and other sceptical member states.
Before the summit, Belgium’s prime minister, Bart De Wever, said Zelenskyy would “probably look everybody straight in the eye and say: thank you for the €90bn, but that money is going to run out because a war is a very costly thing”.
Von der Leyen said the EU had supported Trump’s energy ceasefire “but we have seen that Russia did not respect it, not a single minute” and instead had escalated its attacks. She said the EU intended to increase pressure on Russia, promising a 22nd round of sanctions and adding: “We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war.”

items.content:
In Alaska campaign rally, Trump and Sullivan say Iran war is worth the cost to Americans
A U.S. Air Force E-3 Sentry AWACS aircraft refuels from a KC-135 Stratotanker aircraft during Operation Epic Fury, March 31, 2026.
At a rally in Wasilla on Tuesday, President Donald Trump and Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan said America’s war with Iran is worth the resulting increased cost of fuel and food for Americans.
“No matter what it is, it’s a small price to pay for stopping them from having a nuclear weapon,” Trump said of Iran.
Fuel prices have risen in Alaska and the United States at large since Trump began the Iran war alongside Israel on Feb. 28. According to the latest available state report, heating fuel prices in rural Alaska climbed to an average of $8 per gallon by August, up from $6.49 per gallon in January.
Sullivan has voted 14 times against War Powers Act resolutions that could limit or end American involvement in it.
Before the current war, Sullivan supported the Trump-ordered bombing of Iran last year and has advocated military action against the country.
Speaking on Tuesday in Wasilla, Sullivan said the best way to reduce fuel costs in Alaska is to produce more oil and gas locally, and he said Alaskans should re-elect him because national Democrats oppose oil and gas development.
“It’s important to remember this: the best way to address Alaska’s energy challenges is to produce more Alaskan energy by and for Alaskans,” Sullivan said.
“Ladies and gentlemen, the conflict in the Middle East is temporary. The true forever war is the national Democrats’ war against Alaska oil and gas and our jobs. That’s the forever war,” he said.
Sullivan, the incumbent Republican, is in a close race against Democratic challenger Mary Peltola, who has criticized Trump for starting the war and Sullivan for supporting it.
“We should be standing up to the president, and there have been many times where the Senate and the House have said no to the administration on wars. Where is our backbone?” Peltola said during an Anchorage forum on Oct. 8.
Peltola and Sullivan are in a four-person general election that also includes Dan J. Sullivan of Petersburg and Republican Gerald Heikes of Palmer.
Speaking on Tuesday, Trump said, “We’re very close to winning — I mean, we’ve — I think we’ve won the war because they will — Iran will not have a nuclear weapon, let me put it that way. That war is going to end very soon and when it does, your prices are going to come tumbling down. They already are.”
National and state data has not shown a significant decline in fuel prices over the past month, and consumer price inflation in September was 3.7% , up from August.
In a visit to Fairbanks earlier this month, Vice President J.D. Vance offered comments similar to the ones that Trump made this week, including statements to the effect that Democrats are the enemy.
Peltolta said it’s outrageous to call half of Americans an enemy.
“No American is my enemy. … No Republican is my enemy. No Democrat is my enemy. No Alaskan who is independent, nonpartisan, undeclared is my enemy,” Peltola said.
She seemed to also rebut a New York Times article stating that she once wished a local Planned Parenthood board member would die of a botched abortion: “I have not one person I wish ill will or malice or injustice to in all of Alaska and all of America. We are all in this together. There is no reason to create division amongst ourselves.”
With Sullivan remaining behind in Alaska, Trump repeated his Wasilla message at rallies in Arizona and Montana the following day.
The President has been campaigning nationwide in an effort to boost Republican candidates in the November general election.
“That’s going to end very soon,” Trump said on Wednesday morning in Bullhead City, Arizona, of the Iran war. “And when that ends, your gasoline is going to go down to even lower than it was before it started.”
“If they had a nuclear weapon, within 24 hours they would use it. They’ll knock out the Middle East. Then they’ll start hitting us on the West Coast. They’ll hit Europe because they’re crazy. They’re crazy people. So, this is a very small price people pay. And I thought it would go up much higher,” Trump said of fuel prices.
Later that day, in Kalispell, Montana, Trump gave similar remarks.
“We had the greatest economy in the history of our country in my first administration. We are going to blow it away in this administration, as soon as — as soon as Iran — Iran is going to be over very quickly,” he said.
Oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, south of Iran, have risen in recent months but have not yet returned to pre-war levels.
On the same day as Trump’s remarks in Arizona and Montana, two commercial ships sank in the Strait of Hormuz south of Iran, and CNN reported that the United States is considering whether to attack Iran with the largest non-nuclear bomb in its arsenal.
While Sullivan and Trump are aligned on Iran, they differ in their opinions on Russia and its president, Vladimir Putin.
Sullivan has called Russian President Vladimir Putin a dictator, the leader of a mafia regime, and an authoritarian. Trump has called Putin a friend .
In a TV interview before Tuesday’s rally, the President was asked about their difference of opinion.
“Well, look, I have to make deals with people, so I don’t go around calling them names. I’m a dealmaker; I’ve always been a very good dealmaker. I became very rich because of deals, so I don’t go around mocking people,” he said.
Trump has issued orders that allow Russia to export diesel fuel, possibly lowering global prices but contributing to Russia’s war against Ukraine. Members of Congress, including Sullivan and Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, have criticized Trump’s decision , but the President defended his choice in the interview.
“It’s not oil coming to us, and it’s diesel, which you need. I feel that it’s great because it’s released to the world,” Trump said.

items.content:
Join War on the Rocks and gain access to content trusted by policymakers, military leaders, and strategic thinkers worldwide.
As China and India have improved their relations in recent months, many observers have attributed this improvement to the end of U.S. strategic altruism toward India. Indeed, in the past year, China has watched India lose its balance and simmer in a sense of strategic disorientation due to America's change of heart. Delegation after delegation of Indian strategists visited China, trying to mend ties in search of balance in the Chinese view. Many Chinese experts see India as returning to middle-power alignment for " economic authority and strategic freedom ," which translates into vigorous outreach to Europe, Japan, Canada, and all the middle powers. It's almost as if India is returning to its middle-power roots. The Chinese reassessment of India's power status and its strategic malleability — the extent to which its choices can be shaped — and predictability has significant implications for understanding future dynamics between the two powers. The renewed improvement in ties raises questions about its sincerity and limits. While China recalibrates its relations with India, it is also building fences and chokeholds, first and foremost through supply chain dependence. It is unclear what future policy the next U.S. administration will pursue toward either China or India. Both powers therefore keep their options open.
These assessments reflect ongoing research on China's role in South Asia. They draw on 10 research trips to China, as well as roundtables and exchanges held online and in Washington with Chinese experts since January 2025. China demonstrates a strong tendency toward binary judgments on India's alignment choice, while the reality is far more nuanced, as U.S. policy should be.
In the Chinese policy discourse on India, the first and foremost question has always been India's power status: Is India a great power, or is it simply a middle power with great-power potential? While India's gross domestic product has consistently been a fraction of China's, its claim to great-power status has had major sway over China's calculus. Vishwa Guru — "India the world's guru" — is a famous slogan created under the government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi that, in the Chinese view, best represents India's strategic aspiration: India not only aspires to be a world-class great power but also sees itself as superior and therefore will teach all the other great powers. Although Chinese policymakers do not have romantic misperceptions of India's actual power status, India's aspiration and, even more so, its boldness have been no small shock to Chinese policymakers, who follow the tradition of overestimating adversaries' capacity and hiding their own strength （料敌从宽，判己从严）. India's bold statement made Beijing question whether it underestimated fundamental aspects of Indian capability and potential that warranted India's great-power status.
More importantly, during the first Trump administration and the Biden administration, China stopped questioning India's great-power status. India played a pivotal role in America's Indo-Pacific strategy during these eight years, to the extent that Washington "hyped India's power status" （大肆吹捧印度） and "exaggerated India's development potential."（夸大其发展潜力）
America's willingness to elevate India to a global great power and its seemingly endless provision of assistance to lift India up changed China's original view that only real comprehensive national power mattered. India's gross domestic product has been only about 20 percent of China's and has been unlikely to catch up any time soon to become China's peer. However, that could entirely change if American support continues. Beijing knows this too well because China had been the beneficiary of similar American support and elevation from the 1970s to the 2000s. The difference for China is that back then the United States supported China to counter the Soviet Union, and during the first Trump and Biden administrations, the United States lent similar support to India to counter China. The lesson for China is that great-power status does not actually have to be expressed in real, current terms rather than future expectations and potentials, and U.S. support could very realistically and rapidly elevate India to a new height and single-handedly make India a new great power.
Seeing India as an aspirational and rising power, China believes it followed a policy of accommodation with India throughout this period and beyond. General Secretary Xi Jinping continued outreach and friendly messaging to Modi, including in 2018 (right after the Doklam standoff in 2017); in 2024 at the Kazan summit of the expanded economic bloc originally formed by Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa; and in 2025 when hosting Modi at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit. China did not pursue reciprocal, retaliatory economic policies toward India after 2020. Even on the issue of visas, Chinese officials cited the 280,000 visas China issued to Indian nationals in 2025 to highlight the 2,000 visas India issued to Chinese nationals during the same period to demonstrate the vastly different treatments. For China, these are all reflections of its unwillingness to completely sour ties with India.
But now, with India losing America's favor, India's great-power status has become much less persuasive. Chinese strategists are returning to the view that perhaps, after all, India is just a middle power. It has great potential, but elements in the Indian strategic culture pose irremovable obstacles and consistently sabotage its ascension.
India's Strategic Unmalleability and Predictability
As Chinese strategists observe the fluctuation of ties between the United States and India in the past nine years, it is unsettling and reassuring at the same time. The vast scope and depth of what the United States and India could jointly achieve materially and in practice is unsettling for China, exacerbating China's anxiety about India's future alignment or alliance with the United States and how it could undermine China's roles and aspirations. However, the limitations to what the United States could persuade India to do, even with great rewards and strategic benefits promised, are reassuring for Beijing.
For example, despite the favors and support the United States is willing to provide India, India has refused to abandon its strategic autonomy. At the height of the Russo-Ukrainian War and American demand for India to cooperate, India refused to abandon economic and energy ties with Russia. In private conversations, India's foreign policy community firmly distinguished between "like-minded" and "same-minded" countries to protect its strategic autonomy, and Indian diplomats vehemently emphasized issue-based alignments rather than permanent, rigid alliances.
For China, this is cognitively incomprehensible, as it essentially equates to "India wants to have its cake and eat it, too." If the United States does not have full confidence in Indian loyalty and support, why would the United States spend its valuable resources to do India the favor and let India run with its own agenda? If the answer is a shared U.S.-Indian aspiration to curtail China's rise and expansion, India's expressed reluctance to support the United States and confront China militarily on China's western flank in a future Taiwan contingency, a position that was reiterated amply in track two dialogues, has certainly made the case of "strategic altruism" less appealing for the United States.
On the drastically different interpretations of U.S. support and Indian reactions, all of the China and India specialists I spoke with refer to the Indian concept of " Dānā " (almsgiving) to explain what they see as India's "ungratefulness." What the United States identified as strategic altruism, India sees as strategic egoism because, in Indian culture, the concept of almsgiving views the recipient as doing a favor to the giver by providing them an opportunity to clear negative karma and practice detachment. Following this logic, Indian acceptance of U.S. assistance is India doing the United States a favor, and the United States should be in debt to India consequently. The correctness of this Chinese argument is debatable, but Chinese specialists' unanimous claim of this cultural reading of a religious tradition as the origin of Indian strategic behavior is certainly noteworthy.
Essentially, China perceives India's strategic choice as unmalleable, which significantly, or even critically, undercuts India's potential. Despite the amount of support the United States was willing to supply, India has adhered to its strategic autonomy and refuses to alienate Russia or support a U.S. military campaign against China. Similarly, despite the amount of accommodation China sees itself as willing to provide India, including in economic cooperation, India also adheres to its longstanding position and refuses to forge closer ties. That means India's strategic choice is predictable and cannot be shaped by the enticement of rewards or the threat of punishments. That substantially reduces the strategic value of India as a U.S. partner in strategic competition with China, and consequently, China's anxiety about India's alignment with the United States. Meanwhile, because of the expected limitation to India's cooperation with the U.S. on the latter's competition with China, it also considerably decreases India's strategic appeal for China to pursue.
Once the strategic questions of India's power status and its alignment choices are answered, China's remaining choices concern tactical approaches. With diplomatic engagement and maneuvering ongoing, China is most confident in the supply chain dependence it has built up vis-à-vis India. This is primarily prevalent in trade rather than investment, as India's stringent domestic investment environment and the restrictions on Chinese investment have made investment an unlikely candidate to boost bilateral relations.
Trade tells a very different story. It is in fact profitable for China, especially considering the overwhelming trade surplus China runs vis-à-vis India. In fiscal year 2025 to 2026, the total bilateral trade volume reached $151.1 billion, but India ran a $112.1 billion trade deficit. That means 87 percent of bilateral trade consisted of Chinese exports to India. The trade imbalance is therefore a prominent sore spot for India.
What China has identified, however, is India's middle position in the global supply chain. The argument is that India primarily imports from China materials, parts, and equipment that Indian companies use to make finished products for export to developed-country markets. The deficit India runs vis-à-vis China translates into a trade surplus it runs with other trading partners, such as the United States. India's economic dependence on China, therefore, is already established despite New Delhi's efforts to reduce supply chain risks associated with China. Decreasing India's dependence on China will create significant economic pain for Indian industries and companies. The same supply shock the United States experienced in 2025 in the tariff war with China will happen to India if New Delhi attempts to shut Chinese products out. This economic dependence alleviates China's anxiety over India's strategic autonomy and hostility, as it creates more leverage for China
The other distinct aspect of China's economic relations with India is the missing element of "empowerment," which is prevalent in China's ties with the rest of the South Asian subcontinent. "Empowerment" has been a pillar of China's Belt and Road Initiative engagement in developing countries, meaning China not only trades and invests in the recipient countries, but also utilizes trade, new productive forces, infrastructure development, and industrial cooperation to empower local economies from within. Examples include agricultural technology transfers in Nepal, green technology and the digital economy in Pakistan, and campaigns such as "Smart Bangladesh." However, "empowerment" is not an element in China's economic engagement with India, which raises the question of whether China deliberately avoids economic engagement that could elevate India's technological productivity, industrial upgrading, or high-tech development. One could say India rejects it from China anyway, but the lack of Chinese intention is obvious.
Predicting the future of Chinese-Indian relations is both easy and difficult. It is easy because bilateral relations have a ceiling, considering the many stressors from Pakistan to border disputes to regional competition to complicated geopolitical factors. It is hard because they could have no floor, given the potential for deterioration and the history of war, conflicts, and skirmishes between the two. For the time being, bilateral relations are stabilizing and improving, but their sustainability is subject to at least two unpredictable factors.
The first factor is Indian domestic politics , especially the relationship between the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and the future successor to Modi. Despite the RSS being the parent and ideological guide of the ruling BJP, Chinese observers have noted growing tensions between Modi and the RSS due to electoral friction and the centralization of power and control by Modi. The recent trip by RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat to the United States is seen as a sign of the organization's growing desire to raise its profile. No matter who the next prime minister will be, that person is unlikely to command the vast popularity and persuasiveness Modi has enjoyed. As such, India's future internal cohesiveness and foreign policy appeal remain a question for China.
The bigger uncertainty in Chinese-Indian relations goes back to the United States. Washington's current India policy has taken a dramatic turn, but future shifts in the post-Trump era are also a high-probability event. There is no guarantee that the United States will not resume its competitive strategy vis-à-vis China and once again see India as a needed partner in the process. China believes that India is also waiting for the United States to change its approach again — therefore, nothing current is set in stone. The result is that neither China nor India will be willing to lock in their future strategic posture. Keeping options open remains the optimal approach, but that also means the current rewarming of ties may have an expiration date sooner than people realize.
These assessments have considerable implications for U.S. policy. If Chinese anxiety about the American-Indian relationship has genuinely diminished, then the deterrent value Washington derived from that relationship has diminished with it, which is a cost of the current policy that nobody is counting. If the Chinese read of Indian unmalleability is correct, then a post-Trump return to competition with China, and hence a return to cooperation with India, would face the same limits that frustrated the previous approach, and American planners should develop realistic expectations.
However, a more careful reading of the record also offers a more nuanced position on China's largely binary interpretation of Indian "malleability versus unmalleability." India by and large still holds significant skepticism and concern regarding China's intentions, capabilities, and influence. Despite U.S. dissatisfaction with India's lack of reciprocity, it would be erroneous to assume India's position has not moved at all, such as on defense procurement and the issue of Taiwan. The subtlety does not lie in whether things change, but to what degree. The takeaway is that the United States and India will have to resort to much more careful calibration and negotiation over the terms of their agreement, rather than throwing possible future cooperation entirely out of the window. In March 2026, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau issued a blunt warning during the Raisina Dialogue that the United States would not repeat its "China mistake" with India. The delicacy, however, lies in the cost-benefit analysis, as most policy options are about the measurement of relative losses and gains, rather than an absolute, binary, black-or-white answer.
Yun Sun is the director of the China Program at the Stimson Center.

Broadcom Falls 4% as CEO Hock Tan’s Capital Warning Hangs Over AI Chips; Marvell Drops 4%
Broadcom (AVGO) fell 3% and Marvell (MRVL) dropped 4% after Hock Tan warned capital shortages could become AI's next binding constraint.
NVIDIA's general-purpose accelerators serve far more customers than AVGO or MRVL, limiting its exposure if large cloud buyers cut AI spending.
Multi-year custom chip contracts support Broadcom's bull case, but a capital crunch at concentrated cloud customers could push expected revenue into future years.

A blunt warning about AI funding from one of the chip industry's most prominent executives is hitting custom AI chip stocks harder than the wider semiconductor group. Broadcom ( NASDAQ:AVGO ) stock has dropped 4%, recently trading at $332.10. Meanwhile, Marvell Technology ( NASDAQ:MRVL ) stock is also down 4% and trades at $231.12.
Justin Sullivan / Getty Images Shares of Broadcom and Marvell are trailing the funds that track their corners of the market. The iShares Semiconductor ETF ( NASDAQ:SOXX ) is down 2.7%, a softer decline than either Broadcom stock or Marvell stock. Large-cap tech is holding up better (though it's still selling off), with the Invesco QQQ Trust ( NASDAQ:QQQ ) down 2.3%.
MRVL Price Target — 24/7 Wall St. Hock Tan Flags Capital as AI's Next Bottleneck
Broadcom CEO Hock Tan spoke at an event in Singapore. Earlier this week, he stated that investors "set very extreme expectations only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino." Tan also warned that a shortage of capital could overtake chips and memory as the AI industry's next constraint. That second remark carries the most weight for Broadcom stock and Marvell stock, because it points at the money behind AI data centers.

Broadcom and Marvell design custom AI chips for a small number of large cloud customers under multi-year programs. That structure gives Broadcom and Marvell long visibility into demand, and it also ties each to a short list of buyers, so even one of those customers pulling back on funding could hurt Broadcom and Marvell more than it would a supplier with a wider customer base.
NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA ) makes general-purpose AI accelerators that run across a wide range of customers and workloads. Its approach contrasts with the custom programs at Broadcom and Marvell, where each chip is designed around one buyer's specific needs.
The Invesco QQQ Trust counts Broadcom, Marvell and NVIDIA among its holdings, alongside a much wider mix of large-cap names outside the chip industry. Such a spread makes the Invesco QQQ Trust a broader gauge of large-cap tech than the iShares Semiconductor ETF, and memory, equipment and software names in the fund respond to different drivers than custom chip designers like Broadcom and Marvell do.
The bullish argument for Broadcom depends on custom chip programs that customers sign years in advance. Those commitments give Broadcom a revenue path that one conference remark doesn't change. Custom designs also take years to develop, which raises the cost for any customer that wants to replace Broadcom with another supplier.
On the bear side, the risk for Broadcom is that the capital shortage Tan described reaches the customers paying for those chips. Large cloud buyers facing reduced funding could stretch out deployment schedules, and a concentrated customer list leaves Broadcom with fewer ways to offset that. Even a modest delay could push revenue Broadcom expected in one year into the next.

Tan's warning moves the AI chip debate from hardware supply to customer funding. Broadcom and Marvell now face the question of whether their large cloud customers keep financing AI buildouts at the pace those multi-year programs assume. Any sign that cloud buyers are cutting spending plans could pressure Broadcom stock and Marvell stock again.
Both stocks are falling harder than both funds. That is a sign the market is treating the capital warning as a specific risk for custom chip designers. For investors who share the bull case, a moderate position size makes sense, given the uncertainty Tan raised.

S&P 500 Futures Gain After Warsh’s Remarks; Chip Stocks Extend Slide
Wall Street sign in lower Manhattan New York by Stuart Monk via Shutterstock December S&P 500 E-Mini futures (ESZ26) are up +0.14% this morning as sentiment improved after Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh avoided signaling his near-term policy intentions at an IMF meeting.
Mr. Warsh participated in a roughly half-hour fireside chat with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva at the IMF's meeting in Bangkok on Friday morning. Still, he offered no guidance on near-term monetary policy. "I don't pre-judge meetings, I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year… It's a new chapter at the Fed, and we're not in that business anymore," Warsh said.

'I Can Support My Family By Working Three Days A Week': Jeff Bezos Says Al Gains Will Be So Big Families Won't Need 2 Full-Time Earners
At 97, Charlie Munger Borrowed $37 Million to Go All-In on Alibaba — 2 Years Later He Called It One of the 'Worst Mistakes' of His Life

Traders took Warsh's remarks as another sign the Fed is unlikely to rush into raising rates at its meeting later this month. U.S. rate futures were pricing in a 14.9% chance of an October hike, down from 28% a day earlier.
"The most important thing was what [Warsh] didn't say. Markets took the lack of hawkishness as good news," according to Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid.
On the negative side, chip and AI infrastructure stocks remained under pressure in pre-market trading, failing to join the rebound among their Asian and European peers. Micron Technology (MU), Sandisk (SNDK), and Intel (INTC) each fell more than -1%.
Meanwhile, the price of WTI crude was little changed on Friday as traders weighed plans by the International Energy Agency to speed up the release of emergency oil reserves against lingering Middle East supply risks.
Investors are now awaiting the Federal Reserve's industrial production report.
In yesterday's trading session, Wall Street's major indices ended mostly higher as investors rotated out of chipmakers and into a wider range of stocks as well as bonds. Software stocks climbed, with Intuit (INTU) and ServiceNow (NOW) rising over +6%. Also, defensive healthcare stocks gained, with Alnylam Pharmaceuticals (ALNY) climbing over +4% and Eli Lilly (LLY) rising more than +3%. In addition, International Paper (IP) surged over +6% and was among the top percentage gainers in the S&P 500 after the company said it was in discussions with potential buyers for its Europe, Middle East, and Africa packaging business following unsolicited approaches. On the bearish side, chip and AI infrastructure stocks slid, with Applied Materials (AMAT) and Lam Research (LRCX) dropping more than -3%.
Market participants also parsed a flurry of U.S. economic data on Thursday. items.title: The Stock Market Has Seen This Happen Only 2 Other Times in Over 150 Years, and History Has an Ominous Warning for Investors - The Motley Fool
items.summary: The Stock Market Has Seen This Happen Only 2 Other Times in Over 150 Years, and History Has an Ominous Warning for Investors  The Motley Fool
items.content:
The stock market is entering the fifth year of the current bull market, which started in October 2022. During these past four years, the S&P 500 has surged nearly 120%, fueled by the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.
However, the question on many investors' minds is how much longer the good times can last. There are certainly signs the bull market could be losing steam. The breadth of market winners is actually quite narrow, with only a handful of stocks helping power the index. In fact, over a quarter of stocks in the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -1.15% ) are actually down 40% or more from their all-time highs, while nearly 60% of S&P 500 stocks are below their 200-day moving average .
Meanwhile, renowned investors like Michael Burry, who correctly called the housing bubble, and billionaire hedge fund manager Ray Dalio have been predicting that the AI bubble will burst. Burry has been very vocal, shorting several popular AI stocks, including Nvidia , Micron Technology , and Palantir Technologies , while comparing the current market to before the 2000 dot-com bubble. Dalio, meanwhile, has said the AI boom shows classic signs of a bubble ready to burst.
One of the strongest indicators that the current bull market could be coming to an end is the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio . Created by Yale economist Robert Shiller in 1988, it measures the value of the S&P index relative to its 10-year average inflation-adjusted earnings. The purpose of this is to smooth out periods of earnings boom and bust cycles.
The valuation metric currently sits above 40, which is its second-highest level ever. The only two other times the CAPE ratio has moved above 32 were right before the Great Depression in 1929, when it reached 32.6, and during the dot-com bubble, when it peaked at 44.2. Both times the CAPE hit these levels, huge market corrections followed.
How investors should prepare for a potential market correction
Given the current warning signs in the market, it may seem like the common-sense thing to do would be to sell stocks and step to the sidelines. However, this would likely be a bad decision, as trying to time the stock market rarely works, and even if it does, then you'd have to correctly time getting back in as well. Miss out on some of the largest days in the stock market, and your investment returns could suffer significantly.
For example, Hartford Funds found that 76% of the market's best days have happened during a bear market or the first two months of a bull market, and if you missed the 10 best days in the market over the past 30 years, your return would be cut in half.
Instead, I prefer to follow the advice of legendary investor Peter Lynch , who generated an astonishing 29.2% average annual return while running Fidelity's flagship Magellan Fund. In a 1995 interview with Worth magazine, he said:
Far more money has been lost by investors preparing for corrections or trying to anticipate corrections than has been lost in corrections themselves. ... [i]n the long run it doesn't matter much whether your timing is good or bad. What matters is that you stay invested in stocks.
In the same article, Lynch used the example that if you had invested $2,000 in the S&P 500 every year on Jan. 1 from 1965 until the time the article was written in 1995, you'd have an 11% yearly return. However, if you were unlucky enough to invest at the market peak each year, your return would only drop to 10.6%.
The lesson is ultimately that the best way to prepare for a potential market crash is to not prepare at all. You'll be far better off in the long term consistently dollar-cost averaging into an index exchange-traded fund (ETF)  like the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF ( VOO -1.21% )  than trying to time a potential market crash.
