items.title: The Stock Market Is Doing Something for Only the 3rd Time in 156 Years, and History Is Clear a Crash May be Hiding in Plain Sight - The Motley Fool
items.summary: The Stock Market Is Doing Something for Only the 3rd Time in 156 Years, and History Is Clear a Crash May be Hiding in Plain Sight  The Motley Fool
items.content:
The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -1.15% ) has been on an impressive run since the bear market of 2022. Since hitting a bottom in October 2022, the index has more than doubled, gaining approximately 115%. This translates into an annualized return of roughly 21% over four years, more than twice its historical average of approximately 10% annually, including dividends.
Here's the catch: Stock prices do not outperform their long-term averages indefinitely. Eventually, markets experience mean reversion, a process in which unusually strong returns are followed by periods of weaker performance. While this doesn't guarantee a crash is imminent, one particular valuation indicator is flashing a warning investors should not ignore.
The S&P 500 CAPE ratio is entering dangerous territory
The cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio (CAPE) measures the S&P 500's price relative to its average inflation-adjusted earnings over the last 10 years. The point is to smooth out temporary earnings fluctuations, providing a more balanced perspective on whether stocks are expensive or fairly valued.
Historically, the CAPE ratio has averaged around 17.8. But as of October 2026, readings are hovering around 41. To appreciate how unusual this is, consider some history.
Before the 1929 stock market crash, the CAPE ratio approached 33. The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI -0.51% ) subsequently lost 89% of its value between 1929 and 1932.
In more recent history, the CAPE ratio exceeded 40 in 1999 and peaked near 44 before the dot-com bubble collapse. From March 2000 through October 2002, the S&P 500 declined 49%, while the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -2.08% ) plunged 77%.
Today's CAPE reading above 40 puts stock valuations in rare territory, suggesting the current market is historically expensive. Much like the internet revolution, generative AI promises to transform entire industries, leading investors to pay premiums for companies expected to dominate the future. But I see one important difference between today's AI boom and the dot-com bubble.
During the late 1990s, investors poured unprecedented sums into speculative technology companies with little revenue, no profits, and untested business models. Today's AI leaders are considerably different.
Nvidia ( NVDA -1.05% ) sells the graphics processing units (GPUs) that power much of the AI revolution. Despite its stock price appreciation over the last few years, Nvidia's earnings have also expanded as demand for its chips continues to accelerate.
Meanwhile, Micron Technology ( MU -4.00% ) is benefiting from soaring demand for high bandwidth memory (HBM) and advanced DRAM solutions. Alphabet ( GOOGL -2.33% ) ( GOOG -2.06% ) has combined an established, highly profitable advertising business with an expanding cloud infrastructure and AI services ecosystem.
These businesses aren't selling investors a vision of the future. They're actually generating consistent AI-driven revenue and profits today. This is why their forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios look reasonable relative to what the broader market's CAPE ratio might suggest.
The crack I see is that future growth in the AI landscape hinges on the overarching assumption that big tech will continue spending at historical levels on AI infrastructure. According to Morgan Stanley , capital expenditures (capex) among the five major hyperscalers -- Microsoft , Amazon , Alphabet, Meta Platforms , and Oracle -- are projected to approach $800 billion in 2026, climb to $1.2 trillion in 2027, and reach $1.4 trillion in 2028.
Those investments are an enormous opportunity for Nvidia, Micron, and other semiconductor suppliers. But they also create a financial opportunity cost. Every dollar AI hyperscalers spend building data centers is one that cannot also be used to fund share repurchases or dividend increases. If AI infrastructure investments fail to deliver attractive returns on aggressive timelines, Wall Street could eventually question whether these budgets were justified.
The combination of outsize gains over the last four years fueling historically elevated valuations suggests the market has less room for disappointment. This is why taking some profits right now could make sense. In particular, for investors whose portfolios have become heavily concentrated in AI-related technology stocks, trimming some of your biggest winners could prove wise.
Of course, selling everything would be a questionable decision. Instead, I'd consider maintaining exposure to AI through a more diversified cohort of businesses. Industrial companies stand to benefit from data center construction, electrical equipment, and automation, while energy companies can profit from rising demand for electricity and natural gas. Meanwhile, utilities should benefit from investments in power generation and transmission infrastructure.
The biggest mistake investors can make right now is assuming that historically expensive valuations mean a crash is right around the corner. The CAPE ratio is a useful indicator of long-term expected returns, but it does not have a track record of predicting precisely when corrections will occur.

items.content:
SpaceX rival Eutelsat up 18% as Ukraine's Starshield limits raise fears
Eutelsat soared again on Friday after competitor SpaceX's Starlink systems came under criticism.
Ukrainian officials said the system, which is critical to its defense against Russian attacks, was restricted.
Eutelsat is known as Europe's answer to SpaceX and aims to challenge its market dominance.
A satellite dish in a ground network of satellites at Eutelsat's Madeira office. Photographer: /Bloomberg via Getty Images
Shares of French Satellite Group Eutelsat soared this week as SpaceX 's Starshield drew criticism after the Ukrainian military's access to its systems was suddenly restricted.
Earlier this week, tensions rose between the U.S. and Ukraine after Kyiv accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on its military-grade Starlink internet service without warning, curbing connectivity and limiting Ukraine's ability to defend itself against Russian attacks.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the U.S., saying "Starlink was switched off" in the middle of the night, preventing Ukrainian drones from intercepting Russian attacks, and ultimately contributing to civilian deaths.
"They knew what they did," Zelenskyy said. "It's not about attack. It's also about defending the lives… People were killed because not enough destroying, not enough interceptors, including interceptors with Starlink, which didn't work."
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk responded by shifting blame on the U.S. government and said that Starshield systems were under Washington and President Donald Trump's control.
Eutelsat shares rose 17.7% on Friday, and were up 25% over the past five days following the news of Starlink's struggles in Ukraine.
Eutelsat's share move this week is more evidence "supporting the sovereign value of European Satellite networks," Deutsche Bank analysts said in a note Thursday. Markets viewed Eutelsat as "the credible Starlink alternative" amid the disruption, they added.
"Whilst we note Eutelsat does offer a global LEO [Low Earth Orbit] constellation, we believe it lacks the scale to offer the number of terminals that Starlink can provide," they added. "We would expect the shares to give up some of the gains."
Eutelsat consolidated with satellite internet provider OneWeb in 2023, looking to challenge Starlink's market dominance. However, Eutelsat currently has over 600 satellites in orbit, while Starlink has more than 6,750, the company's websites show.
Ukraine's deputy minister for recovery, infrastructure, and transport Serhiy Derkach told CNBC on Friday that Russia had amped up attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, taking advantage of restrictions on military applications, including striking bridges, railway networks, and border crossings.
"With U.S. limiting the use of Starlinks on the battlefield, Russia feels that this is their moment to try and inflict even more pain and suffering on Ukraine's civilian infrastructure," Derkach said.
"We are definitely moving towards very harsh weeks and months and need our partners' support now more than ever," he said, adding that Ukrainians already experience blackouts lasting 4-12 hours per day.

State regulators approve nearly $140M rate hike for Consumers Energy natural gas customers
The Michigan Public Service Commission has approved nearly $800 million in rate hikes for Consumers Energy since 2020
State regulators approved a $139.2 million annual natural gas rate increase for Consumers Energy — down from the utility’s original request for $240 million
Starting Nov. 1, Consumers Energy customers will see a 4.3% rate increase on their natural gas bills, amounting to approximately $4 per month
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel intervened in the case, urging the Commission charged with approving the rate hike to “slash the request by more than half”
Consumers Energy customers in Michigan will be paying more on their utility bills starting next month after state regulators approved a 4.3% rate increase on Thursday.
Under the new rate — which begins on Nov. 1 — households will pay an average of $4 more for natural gas each month, according to the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC).
The latest rate hike will allow the utility to collect an additional $139.2 million per year from its 1.8 million natural gas customers across the state — a 42% reduction from the $240 million Consumers Energy initially requested. The MPSC also approved a 9.8% return on equity, the utility’s profit margin on capital investments.
The utility says the increase is necessary to support investments in the safety and reliability of its natural gas system, and to support projects to replace aging gas mains and service lines.
However, the Michigan Attorney General’s office says it found “several instances” within Consumers Energy’s rate hike application where the company “inflated capital spending projections and included for themselves unreasonable profit margins.”
Related->> Michigan lawmakers push to rein in energy rates, hold utility companies accountable
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel said in a news release on Thursday that she urged state regulators to slash Consumers’ original rate hike request by more than half, arguing that the company shouldn’t be permitted to request a rate hike above 3.5% due to the burden it places on families already facing rising energy costs.
“Utility customers across the State, whether they pay their bill to Consumers Energy or DTE, ask all the time when their energy bills will stop climbing, and it’s clear that the answer is never,” Nessel said. “For nearly eight years my office has worked doggedly to curb these utility rate hikes, and in turn the cases have only grown. Change must come to our current system of annual on-demand rate hikes and our regulatory structure, but the only changes we’ve seen are fatter rates and heavier bills.”
Nessel says recent rate hike requests from DTE and Consumers Energy have included “inappropriate” expenses such as “private jet travel for staff, millions in executive incentive compensation tied to maximizing shareholder returns, and other unsupported expenditures that could not be demonstrated to be reasonable or prudent.”
The MPSC says it did not approve costs that couldn’t be “sufficiently justified,” noting that it did not approve Consumers’ $7.9 million request for transmission pipeline integrity work, citing “a pattern of over-projecting of costs and under-spending on this program.”
State regulators have approved nearly $800 million in rate hikes for Consumers Energy since 2020, according to Nessel’s office. Other rate hike cases currently open before the MPSC include DTE’s electric rate hike request and Upper Peninsula Power Company’s electric rate hike request .
